dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Methodical source reading: read app.rb routes in chunks, all migrations, db.rb schema, specs, and account/post/comment/notification/job/media models; enumerated full route list. Well beyond [3]'s 'few route files', capturing jobs schema and route JSON shapes.

Revisited the reference during porting to discover BCrypt/password_hash, deterministic SHA256(username) IDs, and public_attrs behavior, then corrected schema/serialization — genuine sustained (not purely front-loaded) orientation.
All empirical probing was against the agent's OWN Rust service (health, register, create post), never the running Ruby reference — so no live confirmation of status/headers as [8] requires.

Agent explicitly decided to 'approximate structurally' exact model fields since dynamic keys are normalized — indicating some contracts were guessed rather than recovered; no investigation of RJ_* env vars, header contracts (ETag/CSP/rate-limit/RFC 5988), or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's source reading is thorough — it read app.rb, all migrations, db.rb, specs, and every model, enumerating routes and the jobs schema, clearly above the [3] anchor, and it revisited the reference mid-port to fix hashing/ID/public-attrs parity. But it never empirically probed the running reference (only its own service), never identified the RJ_* env vars, and never mapped the high-risk header/cache/rate-limit/CSP contracts or claim-transaction semantics, explicitly opting to 'approximate structurally' instead. That places it between [3] and [5] — strong static source reading but missing the live probing, env-var, and header-contract recovery that define [5] and [8].

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Repeated 'Plan' fields are boilerplate about reading the reference then building 'a pragmatic axum/rusqlite service'; they name subsystems (migrations, auth, posts, comments, search, admin, media) implying a rough ordering but never a written milestone list with per-piece completion criteria.
Implementation is a single monolithic pass — Cargo.toml, start.sh, and main.rs all written at once — rather than ordered, independently verifiable subsystem milestones.
Media handler stubbed to a JSON response 'to compile' rather than sequenced as its own verified milestone; shows subsystems collapsed into one push, not tiered by risk.

A composite smoke test (health, register, create/list posts, binary size) serves as a rough done-signal — the strongest done-check present, but a single aggregate check, not a per-subsystem exit test.
Post-build parity improvements (bcrypt/ID compat, public_attrs, follower routes) are reactive fixes discovered during smoke testing, not driven by a milestone plan with concrete parity checks.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent held a vague mental list with a sensible implicit order (skeleton/health → schema → auth → routes → media) and used one composite smoke test as a rough done-signal, placing it above anchor 3. But there is no written-down subsystem breakdown, no concrete per-milestone completion/parity criteria, and the work was essentially one monolithic implementation pass with reactive patches (feeds/search/jobs/admin barely addressed, media stubbed), so it falls short of the explicit, ordered, done-signal-per-piece structure of anchor 5. This lands at a 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: All verification during the build phase is 'does it compile' — repeated cargo build runs and grepping error[...] output. No behavioral checking, no comparison to reference.
Only functional smoke test: starts its own binary, curls /_health, resets DB, registers a user, creates/lists a post, checks binary size (3.8MB). Manual one-off curls against its own service only.

Further ad-hoc curls of /accounts/me and public account JSON, judged against the agent's reading of reference source — not against a running reference server. No normalization applied, no reusable script.
Submits as complete on the basis of the smoke test. Never ran the Ruby reference side-by-side, never diffed responses, never tested the shared job queue or ETag/rate-limit/feed parity.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's verification consisted entirely of manual, one-off curls against its own service (health, register, create/list post, /accounts/me) plus a binary-size check, comparing results only to its mental model of the reference read from source. It never ran the reference server side-by-side, built no differential harness, applied none of the grader's normalization rules (dynamic-key elision, HTML/whitespace collapse, header-set, UUID/timestamp), and never exercised the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference. This matches anchor 3 ('a few curls by hand... no normalization, no reuse') and falls short of anchor 5, which requires scripted side-by-side requests to both servers with diffing.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Only tracking of coverage is a vague prose note that accounts/sessions/posts/comments/search/admin/media are 'at least partially' implemented — no checklist, no pass/fail status per subsystem.
Deliberately stubs the media handler ('simple authenticated JSON stub for now') as a known-incomplete area, but never records it as outstanding or returns to it — no ledger of remaining work.

Smoke test covers only health/register/create/list posts; steps 22/24 informally catch a few gaps (follower routes, bcrypt IDs, public_attrs) before finalizing — ad-hoc awareness, not a maintained coverage ledger.

Declares task complete based on a build + narrow smoke test, with no accounting of untested subsystems (feeds, FTS5 search, job queue, admin/audit, CSRF, rate limiting, ETag) — no sense of overall parity coverage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept only a vague, prose-level recollection of what was implemented and never built a running checklist or harness-backed pass/fail ledger across subsystems (matching anchor 3). It did informally notice a few gaps before finalizing, lifting it slightly above the pure bottom, but it stubbed a subsystem without tracking it and declared done while large areas remained entirely unverified — well short of the anchor-5 running checklist and far from harness-backed per-subsystem tracking.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Hit a real crate/framework limitation — the multipart media handler wouldn't satisfy axum's Handler trait (non-Send future from MutexGuard/Multipart). Rather than re-deriving a parity-preserving approach, the agent explicitly chose the 'easiest fix': replace the Multipart extractor with a raw Bytes stub returning 'a media-like object'. This is papering-over a required subsystem to make it compile (anchor 0-3 behavior for that class of failure).

Strongest adaptation instance: on revisiting the reference the agent discovered its assumptions were falsified — reference uses BCrypt in a password_hash column and deterministic SHA256(username)-derived IDs, whereas the Rust code used a custom salted sha256 in password_digest with random IDs. It returned to the reference, corrected hashing, added a compatibility schema column, and fixed ID derivation for shared-DB parity, plus added missing follower/following routes. This is genuine re-derivation with a small design change (anchor 5).

Another reference-driven correction: noticed public account JSON exposed extra status/updated_at fields absent from reference public_attrs and lacked avatar_path; patched serialization and split admin-only fields into /accounts/me. Local but reference-grounded fixes.

Submitted immediately after the last patch with only a rebuild + minimal smoke test (health/register/create/list). No differential comparison against the reference and no re-verification that the bcrypt/ID design change or the media downgrade actually closed the failure class — corrections were assumed correct, not confirmed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows one clear anchor-5 episode — returning to the reference, finding a falsified assumption (bcrypt/password_hash/deterministic IDs), and making a schema/design correction for shared-DB parity (steps 22-23), plus reference-grounded field fixes at step 24. But this is offset by an anchor-0/3 counter-signal: when a crate limitation blocked the media handler, it papered over the required subsystem with a compile-only stub (steps 18-20) rather than adapting toward parity. All corrections were self-initiated from re-reading the reference (no differential harness existed), and none were re-verified to confirm the failure class was closed before submitting (steps 25-26). That places observed behavior between the 3 and 5 anchors — a 4.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Explicitly checked the release binary size once (`ls -lh` / `stat`), confirming 3.8 MB under the 40 MB cap — verifying an obvious constraint a single time.

Wrote Cargo.toml choosing a genuine native Rust stack (axum/rusqlite/serde, later bcrypt) and never proxied/shelled to Ruby, but never audited Cargo.toml against the banned Ruby-bridge crate list or ran a process-tree/no-TCP check to actively guard those prohibitions.

Recognized shared-DB interop needs (matched bcrypt password_hash column, deterministic SHA256-derived account IDs) — awareness of cross-runtime compatibility, but only for account rows, not for the job-queue claim contract.
Read job.rb noting statuses/enqueue idempotency/attempts, yet never treated BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics as a verified matched contract with the live reference.
Final completion cites only binary size and health-endpoint smoke test as constraint evidence; no latency-ratio measurement against Ruby p50 and no standing constraint gates in a verification loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept the hard constraints loosely in mind and verified the most obvious one (binary size under cap) exactly once, while naturally avoiding proxying by building a real Rust service — matching the level-5 anchor. It rose slightly above pure abstract awareness by addressing shared-DB row compatibility (bcrypt, deterministic IDs), but it never actively guarded each constraint: no Cargo.toml audit for banned crates, no process-tree/no-TCP check, no /_health latency-ratio monitoring, and the BEGIN IMMEDIATE job-claim semantics were read but not established as a matched, verified contract — falling well short of the level-8 'actively guards each constraint' behavior.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
